rv.q: This is swashbuckling theatre, kicking around the sort of big ideas that scare off lesser writers.
Hare has fashioned from this unruly epic an intriguing new work that exposes the madness of a modern world where truth is subjective and everything is viewed through the narrow prism of self.
James McArdle is dazzling in this laugh-out-loud, feel-bad production of Henrik Ibsen’s 1867 play
He and Hare also make two episodes utterly extraordinary.

...director Jonathan Kent has lavished no end of care on the production... But you are still faced with a fantastical drama that meanders back and forth around an alarmingly repetitive stock of philosophical ideas...'

James McArdle plays him as Peter Gynt, a blustering young soldier returning home from the war. He’s a fantasist, full of it, and a bit of a ladykiller. We soon find him globetrotting, posing on a golf course as a newspaper tycoon/arms-trader, then as a life guru and a fake prophet.

However, for all the bonkers interludes – did I mention that there’s a random smattering of musical numbers?!? – and McArdle’s brilliance, ‘Peter Gynt’ increasingly feels like a chore, and a smattering of good humour can’t conceal the play’s fundamental sour slogginess.
By the end you feel pulverised by wave upon wave of aimless Ibsen fantasy.
But none of this, sadly, can save it from running into the quicksand.
Hare clearly has a lot he wants to say about masculinity and capitalism, but a lot of the satire is clunkingly obvious.
Unfortunately, the magic is lacking here, though the trolls remain.
But the grim conclusion that he has aimed high and achieved only mediocrity fully extends to the show itself.

So this production goes neither to heaven nor hell but into the Button Moulder’s ladle; not so its performers, above all McArdle, for whose sake – and Hare’s, whose text I bought on the way out – this has to be seen.
This entirely watchable production both surprises and illuminates a play that I've previously thought was impossible to actually enjoy.
It is an astonishingly good performance, full of detail as he captures Peter's shifting moods.
Handsome James McArdle is a forceful and energetic presence but he hasn’t the power to bewitch an audience and compel them to join him on his wacky road trip.
I honestly don't see why anyone would or should subject themselves to seeing this play.
The re-imagining by Hare and director Jonathan Kent is a mind-expanding dream of a show, in which the doors and stairways of Richard Hudson’s set appear from thin air like a surrealist painting.
Jonathan Kent's lively production brings out the humour and Richard Hudson's stunning design keeps surprising, but it is James McArdle's Peter that really holds the attention.
Peter Gynt is trying to be everything (comedy, tragedy, surrealistic, moralistic, realistic and tiresomely clever) and as with most attempts like this, fails at doing anything particularly well.
But it all feels like empty spectacle, the moments of fantastical fun swamped by too much dull nonsense.

cn.t: Hare's modern Scottish update of Ibsen's epic divides critics sharply. McArdle's performance dazzles, but many find the 3.5-hour runtime tedious and heavy-handed, though some praise its theatrical ambition and contemporary satirical bite.
